title: Wall Street Hits Records as Yen Intervention and Earnings Surge Reshape Markets
excerpt: The Dow and S&P 500 reached all-time highs on blockbuster corporate earnings, while a rare joint U.S.-Japan intervention to support the yen exposed the fragile currency dynamics underpinning the global rally.
body:
• The Dow closed at a record 54,085 and the S&P 500 hit 7,736, driven by Q2 earnings growth tracking an extraordinary 47% — nearly double expectations from a month earlier.
  • Japan is estimated to have spent nearly $100 billion in 48 hours on a rare coordinated intervention with the U.S. to support the yen, which had fallen to 40-year lows.
  • The yen carry trade — borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets — has swelled to its largest size in nine years, raising the risk of a sharp unwind if the currency reverses.
  • More than 80% of S&P 500 companies are beating earnings expectations, with AI-driven demand boosting results from tech giants to industrial bellwethers like Caterpillar.

U.S. stock markets charged to new records this week as a powerful earnings season collided with extraordinary central bank intervention in currency markets, producing a rally built on strong corporate fundamentals but shadowed by risks lurking in the global financial plumbing.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 907 points on Tuesday to close at a record 54,085.88, while the S&P 500 gained 1.79% to reach 7,736.52 — also an all-time high. The Nasdaq Composite surged 2.59% to 26,584.99. The pan-European STOXX 600 also hit a record, according to Reuters.

An Earnings Season for the Books

The rally is anchored in corporate results that have exceeded even the most optimistic projections. Aggregate annual S&P 500 profit growth is tracking at 47.7% in Q2, according to LSEG data — nearly double what analysts expected a month ago. More than 80% of reporting companies are beating earnings estimates.

The strength is broad-based. Caterpillar raised its annual revenue forecast, citing demand from AI data center construction. Palantir Technologies surged after lifting its own guidance. Amazon hit a $3 trillion market capitalization.

"There's a general sense of optimism out there and that's being reflected."

— Oliver Pursche, Senior Vice President, Wealthspire Advisors

Yen Intervention: A $100 Billion Gamble

Beneath the equity rally, a dramatic currency battle unfolded. Japan is estimated to have spent nearly $100 billion over 48 hours last week buying yen in a coordinated intervention with the U.S. Treasury — the first American participation in Japanese FX markets in 15 years.

The action pushed the yen from 40-year lows near 164 per dollar to as strong as 155.20, a roughly 5% move in three trading sessions. Two market sources told Reuters the U.S. Treasury bought yen for euros rather than selling dollars, an unusual maneuver designed to support Japan's currency without signaling that Washington wants a weaker greenback.

Japan has now spent an estimated $310 billion defending the yen over the past four years, spanning interventions in 2022, 2024, and 2026. Whether the spending has worked is debatable — the yen may have sunk even further without it — but the sheer scale underscores Tokyo's growing anxiety about currency weakness that raises import costs and fuels inflation.

The Carry Trade Threat

The yen's weakness has fueled a surge in the carry trade, where investors borrow cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets like U.S. tech stocks and Treasuries. Speculative short positions on the yen hit a nine-year high of more than 115,000 contracts in June, according to CFTC data.

The strategy is profitable until it is not. In August 2024, a Bank of Japan rate hike triggered a sudden yen reversal that forced rapid unwinding of carry trade positions, sending shockwaves through global equity and currency markets. The S&P 500 fell sharply over three days.

"It is low volatility until it is not," said Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management. "The trick is not to pretend that intervention cannot happen. It is to avoid picking up nickels in front of it."

Cross-Currents Ahead

The immediate outlook is shaped by competing forces. Record earnings, strong manufacturing data — U.S. factory activity hit a four-year high in July — and falling oil prices on hopes of a diplomatic resolution to the Iran conflict all support risk appetite. But elevated yen short positioning, uncertain Fed policy under Chair Kevin Warsh, and questions about AI spending sustainability create potential tripwires.

For investors in the diaspora with exposure to both U.S. and Asian markets, the week illustrated how interconnected the rally has become — and how quickly currency dislocations can propagate through a system built on leverage and momentum.
